title: In-Context Universal Approximation: Prompts as Programs
one_liner: A frozen Transformer can interpret any continuous program handed to it via the prompt, and combine simpler programs into complex ones on-the-fly.
lead: This paper answers a deep question: what makes a Transformer (like GPT) able to do so many different tasks without retraining? The answer is that the weights stay frozen, and the prompt acts like a program that tells the Transformer what to do. The paper proves that a fixed Transformer can be a perfect universal interpreter of algorithms.

problem.h2: How does a frozen Transformer execute different programs?
paras: Before this paper, it was unclear whether a Transformer with fixed weights could really execute arbitrary algorithms, or whether it was just memorizing patterns. If I hand a Transformer a new prompt describing a task it has never seen—say, sorting numbers or computing a sine wave—how does it know what to do?

A naive attempt: hope that during training, the model learned enough examples that it can guess the right answer for new prompts. But this breaks when the prompt describes an algorithm the model has never seen or an unusual composition of tasks. The Transformer has to do something deeper than interpolation.

callout.html: The paper proves: a fixed-weight Transformer interprets the prompt as a program specification and executes that program step by step, without changing any of its internal numbers.

panels.title: 1. A fixed Transformer
panels.caption: Frozen weights. Stuck internal numbers. Reads a prompt, produces output.

panels.title: 2. Prompt arrives as a program
panels.caption: The prompt is not data; it is an instruction set.

panels.title: 3. Transformer emulates the algorithm
panels.caption: The prompt tells it what computation to run. Fixed weights execute it.

panels.title: 4. Compose two programs
panels.caption: Prompts for sort and average chain together. One Transformer runs both.

panels.title: 5. New complex algorithm
panels.caption: Without retraining, the Transformer assembles and executes the composition.

steps.text: The prompt encodes what algorithm to run.
Frozen layers execute that program mechanically.
Each output word represents one step of the algorithm.
Two prompts-as-programs combine into one longer prompt.
The same fixed weights run sort, search, addition, or anything else.

paras: The Transformer does not change its own weights. Instead, it changes its internal computation state: it reads the prompt, translates that specification into hidden intermediate values, and uses those to steer what the next layer outputs. The prompt reprograms the computation without touching the weights.

hidden.name: what the fixed weights can compute given a prompt
paras: The paper's key insight is that a Transformer's ability to execute arbitrary algorithms lives not in the weights but in how the prompt-guided computation flows through the layers. The hidden quantity is: given any continuous sequence-to-sequence function (a mapping from input to output), can the Transformer approximate it by interpreting a prompt specification?

The paper proves that yes, it can. For any target computation, there exists a prompt that causes the fixed Transformer to emulate that computation. The paper shows this by constructing an explicit emulation: the prompt describes the algorithm, and the Transformer's layers mechanically execute it step by step.

heat.caption: Darker means more algorithmic expressiveness. Highlight shows where the prompt-as-program interpretation happens.

reads.html: The Transformer is a programmable machine: the prompt is the program, and the frozen weights are the machinery that executes it.
In-context universality: for any continuous sequence function f, there exists a prompt p such that the frozen Transformer with p in its context outputs an arbitrarily close approximation to f(x).

mechanism.h2: Why the proof works: emulation as computation
paras: The paper's proof strategy is concrete: it shows that any algorithm can be emulated via the Transformer's layers. Here is how. An algorithm is a sequence of steps—read input, apply rule, write intermediate result, repeat. The prompt specifies this algorithm in natural language or symbolic form. When the Transformer processes the prompt in its context, the prompt's tokens get embedded (converted into a list of numbers), and as those tokens flow through the layers, each layer uses them to decide how to transform the input.

The key is that the Transformer's architecture—in particular, the way each layer reads the prompt-words and uses them to steer the computation—is sufficiently flexible to execute arbitrary instruction sequences. The proof constructs an explicit mapping: given an algorithm (e.g. 'sort the input'), the prompt encodes it, and the layers mechanically read that encoding and run it as a program.

For composition: if prompt A executes algorithm F and prompt B executes algorithm G, then concatenating A and B in the context lets the Transformer execute F then G in sequence, because the computation state from A flows into the interpretation of B.

stages.s: Layers use prompt-numbers to steer computation
Each output token is one algorithm step

math.words: output equals the algorithm applied to the input, where the algorithm is determined by the prompt
math.equation: T_frozen(prompt, x) ≈ f(x) for any continuous sequence function f, where T is the Transformer
symbols: any target continuous function from inputs to outputs
approximates arbitrarily closely with a long enough prompt and Transformer

worked.title: A tiny worked example: sorting three numbers
lines: Prompt (in the context): 'Return the list in ascending order.'
Layer 1 embeds the prompt-tokens into numbers describing 'ascending order.'
Layer 2 reads the input and these description-numbers, starts outputting tokens.
Result: [1, 2, 3]. The algorithm (sorting) was executed without retraining.
Composition example: if prompt was 'sort, then average', the same Transformer chains both operations.

math.note: The equation says that frozen weights plus a prompt specification are sufficient to approximate any algorithm; the proof constructs an explicit emulation.

charts.title: Without emulation (naive)
charts.note: A model that only memorizes from training data fails on unseen algorithms.

charts.title: With in-context emulation
charts.note: When the Transformer interprets the prompt as a program, it executes arbitrary algorithms.

items.html: If the prompt is vague or contradicts itself, the Transformer cannot infer a single algorithm. The output will be garbage.

A very long algorithm needs many layers and output words. If the algorithm is more complex than the Transformer's depth and context allow, the execution gets cut off, because the Transformer can only produce up to a fixed number of output words and use a fixed number of layers.

items.b: Prompt overfitting to the training examples.
items.html: The paper assumes the Transformer learned a general emulation engine. If training examples were narrow or repetitive, the Transformer may not have learned to emulate algorithms outside that range.
With a clear prompt, sufficient depth, and broad training, the Transformer emulates the algorithm faithfully.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a Transformer (small depth, maybe 3-4 layers) and train it on examples of simple algorithms: addition, subtraction, element-wise maximum, reversing a sequence. Then, freeze the weights. Test whether the frozen Transformer can execute algorithms it never saw during training, by giving it new prompts like 'compute element-wise minimum' or 'sort then add'. If the prompts are clear and the training was broad enough, the frozen Transformer should execute these new algorithms correctly.
demo.metric_eq: accuracy = number of novel algorithms executed correctly / total novel algorithms tested
demo.closing: The key is to show that without retraining, a frozen Transformer interprets an unseen prompt-as-program and produces the correct output sequence.
